summary:
Left Behind: Letters from the Silent Explorers is an interactive website that gives a voice to the spacecraft and equipment NASA has left behind. Visitors explore a 3D map of the solar system, where each glowing beacon marks a silent explorer. Choosing one opens a letter written from the machine’s own point of view, telling what it was built to do, what it achieved, and how it went quiet. A “Your turn” tab lets visitors take a quiz, earn badges, and download a card to keep or share.

It answers the challenge by turning discarded NASA equipment on the Moon and Mars, and beyond, into stories people can feel instead of a dry list of facts. Every fact comes from NASA’s public sources, which are listed on the site.

It matters because most people only remember the famous missions. These forgotten machines left behind data, lessons, and physical traces, and their stories help people think about what we leave in space. Hosted on GitHub, the site is free and open to anyone with a browser, including students in Nepal. It was built by Selene Venturers, a team of five first-semester students.
details:
Left Behind: Letters from the Silent Explorers

Space is full of machines we built, launched, and eventually stopped hearing from. We wanted to give them a voice. Left Behind is a website where you explore a 3D map of the solar system, and every glowing beacon on it is a spacecraft or piece of equipment NASA left behind. Choose one and you read a letter written from the explorer’s own point of view: what it was built to do, what it achieved, and how it went quiet.

You can drag to look around, scroll or pinch to zoom, and speed time up or run it backward to watch everything move. A “Real positions” mode shows where things actually are, and there’s a list view if you’d rather browse. We say openly that sizes and distances aren’t to scale, because we chose readability over accuracy there.

The “Your turn” tab is where visitors take part. They take a quiz on what they’ve read, earn badges for their results, and download a card showing what they collected, something they can keep or share with friends.

Most people only remember the famous missions. We wanted to show that the forgotten ones still matter, because they left behind data, lessons, and physical traces. We hope these stories make space history feel personal and make people think about what we leave in space. Because it’s a website hosted on GitHub, anyone can open it without installing anything, including students in Nepal with slow internet.

We built it with [HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js for the 3D map]. All the facts come from NASA’s public websites: NASA (nasa.gov), NSSDCA (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov), JPL (jpl.nasa.gov), Astromaterials Curation (curator.jsc.nasa.gov), and NASA Science (science.nasa.gov). We gathered information from several pages across these sites, and they are all listed on our Sources page.

What makes it creative for us is that we treated equipment like characters and made the map itself the way the story is told. Along the way we weighed accuracy against simplicity, kept the site light enough for low-end devices, checked every fact against NASA sources, and kept the tone respectful without inventing anything.

We are Selene Venturers, five first-semester BSc CSIT and BIT students from Nepal, and we built this within the limited time of the hackathon.
